full_judgment: 10. The High Court Division also found that the defendant No. 1 claimed that most of the land settled in favour of Aparna Charan, his father, were in RS Jote No. 81 but some part thereof was recorded wrongly in the name of Sarada Kripa Lala in RS Jote No. 86 and after coming to know about the same from the defendant No. 2 for the first time in the year 1954 he filed JM Case No. 230 of 1954-55 but the above claim is not correct as there is no corroboration from any witness in this regard and the fact that Aparna Charan did not take settlement of the full CS Plot No. 1748 and took settlement of a part of it is evident from Exhibit F, i.e. the order sheet of Miscellaneous Case No. 284 of 1907-08 for settlement, Exhibit G i.e. the list of tenants, Exhibit H i.e. the kabuliyat executed by Aparna Charan, Exhibit S(6) i.e. sale deed dated 26-7-1939 executed on behalf of the defendant No. 1 in favour of Jibendra Lal Dutta and Exhibit S(7) i.e. the sale deed dated 5-8-1942 executed by Jibendra Lal Dutta in favour of the defendant No. 1 which will show that the Aparna Charan entered into possession of the full CS Plot No. 1748 after demarcation of boundaries in the year 1912 and then, as will be evident from Exhibits A-A4, he retreated to the settled portion of CS Plot No. 1748 at the time of RS operation and was not in possession of RS Plot No. 2956 at the time of preparation of RS records as is evidenced by Exhibit E(1), the RS Khatian No. 776, and that is why RS Plot No. 2956 was recorded in the name of Sarada Kripa Lala who actually possessed the suit property at the time of RS operation and the defendant No. 1 has failed to rebut the presumption of RS records by any documentary or unimpeachable oral evidence and as has been held in the case of Alimuddin Munshi vs Mainuddin Talukder, 14 DLR 725, merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the record of rights, the presumption under the entry is not rebutted and there must be further evidence to show that the entries are incorrect and the defendant No. 1 having failed to produce any documentary evidence or any convincing evidence to show that and further the non-payment of rent by the defendant No. 1 for RS Plot No. 2956 from 1930 to 1955 was not an inadvertence as has been urged and, on the other hand, such non payment supports that the defendant No. 1 and his predecessor had no interest in the suit property and that is why they did not pay rent for the suit property after the RS operation and further from 1930 to 1955 the defendant No. 1 and his predecessor were quite happy and content with the recording of the land settled in favour of Aparna Charan in RS Jote No. 81 and Aparna Charan paid rent for that jote in the justified belief that all the settled lands of Aparna Charan were included in it and several transactions were made in respect of the lands of Jote No. 81 with the clear understanding and belief that those dealings were in respect of the entire settled lands of Aparna Charan and the defendant No. 1 took certified copies of his father's settlement papers, Exhibits F-H in the year 1954 and he failed to show any other certified copy taken before 1954 and further, taking advantage of the moribund condition of the bank in the year 1954, the defendant No. 1 went into possession of the suit property in the year 1955 and showing interpolated Exhibits F-H obtained mutation of the suit property in his own name and started the brick field during Pakistan period as unwittingly given out by DWs 1 and 2 and then he paid rent for RS Jote No. 86 from 1955 onwards and sold 1.20 acres of the suit land to Pakistan Tobacco Co Ltd in the year 1956 and in the year 1965 he stopped manufacturing bricks and on dividing the suit property into many plots started selling those to willing purchasers till an order of status quo was passed by the High Court Division and while the bank has been able to prove that it had possession of the suit land from 1934-55 by documentary evidence and, on the other hand, the defendant No. 1 has no documentary evidence and/or any reliable oral evidence in support of his title and possession of the suit land from 1930-55 and as has been held in the case of Keshav Raghunath Deshpande vs Govind Chimnaji Deshpande, AIR 1928 Bom 287 the fact that a stranger in the present case, the bank takes possession of a property under a mistake common to all does not make his possession any less adverse and it has also been held in a number of cases, namely, Govinda vs Mallayya, 311 C 678, Kunwar Sen vs Darbarilal ILR 38 All 411, Ram Piari vs Budhsen ILR 43 All 164, Priya Sakhi vs Manbodh Bibi, ILR 44 Cal 425, that a mortgagee, who does not enter possession in his character as mortgagee, may by 12 years' adverse possession, acquire a good title against a mortgagor and in a number of cases, namely, Zaibunnessa vs Parichit, 23, IC 611, Mula Singh vs Budh Singh, 25 IC 616, and Bhari vs Abbayanath, 41, IC 862, it has also been held that a mortgagee may by 12 years' adverse possession, acquire a good title to other land of the mortgagor which had not been validly mortgaged to him and that in the present case adverse possession of the bank against Sarada Kripa Lala and his successor started from the date of mutation on 7-11-36 and the bank continued in possession and its possession stood reconfirmed during the requisition and derequisition proceedings in 1942 and 1946-47 and that in the year 1942 the defendant No. 1 re-purchased RS Jote No. 81 being fully satisfied that this was the entire settled land of his father and further, the defendant No. 1 or Sarada Kripa Lala was no where in the picture during the requisition and de-requisition proceedings and therefore taking the date of the possession of the bank to be 7-11-36, the bank acquired good title to the suit land by adverse possession and so Madhabi Lata Lala had no saleable interest in the suit land on 29-9-58 and though Mr Mahmudul Islam, relying on the case of Sarat Chandra Maiti vs Bibhaboti Debi AIR 1921 Calcutta 584, submitted that when a property is requisitioned it passes into legal custody and during the continuance of requisition such custody is for the benefit of the true owner but the above cited case is a case of attachment under section 146, CrPC and there is nothing to show that such an order of attachment under section 146, CrPC is applicable in the case of mortgage.
